content: The sticky layer at the bottom of a container, if present, should be checked for its ability to re-disperse. A simple method to verify this involves probing the bottom of the container with a glass rod or a similar device suited to the container's size and shape. If the formulation has flocculated, it may not be possible to re-disperse this sticky layer. Analytical methods used must comply with CIPAC, AOAC, or equivalent standards. If these methods are unpublished, full details and appropriate validation data must be submitted to FAO/WHO by the proposer. Separate clauses must be provided for each relevant impurity. Clauses addressing the free active ingredient content and the release rate of the active ingredient are required only for encapsulated active ingredients and only if relevant to the intended properties of the capsules. A clause to control the release rate is typically necessary for capsules designed for slow or controlled-release properties. If multiple active ingredients are encapsulated, limits must be specified for each. Methods for determining the free active ingredient and release rate may be product-specific. Homogenization must be performed carefully to avoid aeration of the sample. If both g/kg and g/L at 20°C are required by the buyer, analytical results in case of dispute should be calculated as g/kg. Clauses should include only relevant impurities and be omitted if none exist. Analytical methods must be peer-validated. Percentages may be specified in one or more ranges, as appropriate to the product. Laser diffraction is not always suitable for measuring the particle size distribution of liquid formulations. Dispersion stability tests are typically conducted after stability tests at elevated temperatures. These tests should be performed at a 2% dilution or at the highest and lowest recommended usage rates. Oversized capsules, crystals, agglomerates, or extraneous materials that could block spray nozzles or filters in the spray tank must be avoided. The mass of the sample used in testing should correspond to the highest recommended usage rate. Tests should be conducted in CIPAC standard water D. Mixed formulations of CS and SE (ZE) are stable aqueous dispersions containing microcapsules, solid fine particles, and emulsion droplets, each containing one or more active ingredients. These formulations are intended for dilution in water before spray application. Combining active ingredients in a single formulation eliminates the need for tank mixing, which can lead to incompatibility, and allows for the control of a wider range of pests with fewer applications. Encapsulation of one or more active ingredients serves purposes such as increasing residual biological activity, reducing acute toxicity, or achieving a physically or chemically stable water-based formulation. The purpose of encapsulation determines whether the free active ingredient and release rate are relevant properties of a specific product. For mosquito coils (MC), the material must burn without producing a flame except at the beginning and should be easily extinguishable after ignition. The active ingredient must comply with identity tests, and the average weight of coils, determined from 20 single coils, must not differ from the declared weight by more than ±10%. The average burning time, determined from five single coils burning continuously in a draft-free atmosphere, must not be less than the declared time. Each coil must withstand a minimum load of 120 g without breaking. Twin coils must be properly manufactured to facilitate easy separation, with no more than three coils breaking out of 50 twin coils separated. For vaporizing mats (MV), the mat should consist of a pulp-made or inert material impregnated with an insecticide. Stabilizers, synergists, slow-release agents, perfumes, and coloring agents may be added. The mat is intended for use in a heating unit designed to produce slow volatilization of the active ingredient. The mat size should be compatible with the associated heater. For liquid vaporizers (LV), the product consists of a liquid insecticide formulation in a cartridge or bottle designed to fit a suitable heater unit. The formulation must be effective as it evaporates at a suitable rate over the period claimed by the manufacturer. The cartridge or bottle must minimize the risk of accidental ingestion and be made of heat-resistant material, with a child-proof cap and a stopper to prevent spillage. The wick must be made of a porous, heat-resistant material capable of drawing up sufficient insecticide for vaporization to provide effective protection against mosquitoes. The wick must also be designed to vaporize the total content of the insecticide formulation in the attached cartridge or bottle. The minimum effective period must be declared, and the cartridge or bottle must hold enough formulation to function for at least the declared period. Samples must be stored to prevent deterioration, and sampling instruments must be clean and dry. Random sampling methods should be used, and any defective samples must be identified. The acceptance number represents the maximum permissible number of defective samples for a lot to be accepted.
